transcript.speaker: Alex Rivera
transcript.text: Okay team, the big question for today: do we migrate to React Server Components across the board, or do we keep the hybrid approach for the meeting detail page?

transcript.speaker: Leo Hartman
transcript.text: I've been prototyping RSC for the transcript viewer. Server-side rendering dramatically reduces the initial load time — from 1.4s to under 400ms on a cold page load.

transcript.speaker: Marcus Brody
transcript.text: From the infra side, RSC means more compute on the edge. We'd need to make sure the meeting data fetching doesn't add latency — especially for large transcripts over 200 utterances.

transcript.speaker: Alex Rivera
transcript.text: I think we adopt RSC for static parts of the meeting detail page — header, metadata, transcript viewer. Keep the AI analysis panel as a client component since it has interactive tabs and optimistic state.

transcript.speaker: Leo Hartman
transcript.text: That hybrid architecture makes sense. We already have that split naturally from Commit 2. RSC for data, client for interaction.

transcript.speaker: Marcus Brody
transcript.text: Agreed. Let's also standardize error boundaries — right now a failed analysis fetch causes the whole page to go blank. Not ideal.

transcript.speaker: Alex Rivera
transcript.text: Good point Marcus. I'll add a MeetingErrorBoundary component that shows graceful fallback UI instead of crashing the render tree.

transcript.speaker: Leo Hartman
transcript.text: Can we also talk about the transcript search? Right now it's all in client state. For very long transcripts that could get slow. Should we consider server-side filtering?

transcript.speaker: Alex Rivera
transcript.text: Let's defer server-side search until transcripts actually get long. Right now average is under 50 utterances. Flag it for Commit 4.

transcript.speaker: Marcus Brody
transcript.text: Sounds like a plan. I'll update the infrastructure notes with the RSC adoption decision. Let's move fast.

transcript.speaker: Alex Rivera
transcript.text: Sprint 18 retrospective. Let's go round — what went well, what didn't, and what we improve. Leo, kick us off.

transcript.speaker: Leo Hartman
transcript.text: Went well: we shipped the AI analysis panel on time and it's getting great feedback in internal testing. Didn't go well: I got blocked waiting for API contract alignment for two days mid-sprint.

transcript.speaker: Priya Nair
transcript.text: Designs are moving faster now that we have the component system. The blocker for me was late design feedback — approval cycles took longer than estimated.

transcript.speaker: Elena Rostova
transcript.text: From my side, Sprint 18 was great for content. We drafted the launch announcement and got it reviewed. But I need engineering to flag features at least 5 days before release so I can prep materials.

transcript.speaker: Alex Rivera
transcript.text: That's fair Elena. I'll add a 5-day marketing heads-up as a default checklist item in our release process going forward.

transcript.speaker: Leo Hartman
transcript.text: On the API contract thing — can we start doing 15-minute async API alignment sessions at the start of each sprint to prevent mid-sprint blocks?

transcript.speaker: Alex Rivera
transcript.text: Yes. I'll set up a recurring 15-minute API contract review every Monday morning with Marcus joining async.

transcript.speaker: Priya Nair
transcript.text: For design reviews, let's try a 48-hour feedback SLA. If feedback isn't given in 48 hours, design is considered approved for implementation.

transcript.speaker: Alex Rivera
transcript.text: Love that. Let's document the 48-hour design review SLA in the team handbook. Sprint 19 goal: zero mid-sprint API contract blocks. Let's go.

analysis.executiveSummary:
The Sprint 18 retrospective brought together the frontend and product teams to review successes and operational roadblocks. The team successfully delivered the AI analysis panel on schedule, receiving positive internal feedback. However, several friction points were identified, including mid-sprint API contract delays, lengthy design review cycles, and late feature notifications for marketing.

To resolve these issues, the team established three concrete process improvements: a 5-day marketing advance notification for upcoming features, recurring Monday API alignment sessions to prevent mid-sprint blockers, and a strict 48-hour SLA for design feedback and approvals. These changes form the foundation for Sprint 19, with a primary objective of achieving zero mid-sprint API blocks.
keyTakeaways: The AI analysis panel was shipped on time and received positive internal testing feedback.
Mid-sprint blockers caused by API contract alignment issues hindered frontend development velocity.
Delayed design review cycles slowed down implementation progress.
Marketing requires earlier feature flagging (at least 5 days prior to release) to adequately prepare launch materials.
New process SLAs and recurring alignment syncs were established to streamline cross-functional collaboration for Sprint 19.
